paragraphs: Now, if you ever find yourself standing at the edge of a moonwell in Shadowglen, take a moment before you do anything else. Just look at it. It's so silver and so still that it seems to be quietly correcting the moon's homework, and it has been doing this, patiently, since long before anyone thought to build a path to it.
It was beside this moonwell that Nova stood one morning, reading a note for the third time, as if reading it a fourth time might make it more helpful.
"Conservator Ilthalaine requests your assistance at the moonwell clearing. Bring your staff."
That was all it said. No explanation. No "dear Nova, hope this finds you well." Just an order, politely disguised as a request, the way orders from conservators so often are.

Nova was, by nature, the sort of person who liked to know things before she did them. Not knowing things made her nervous, and being nervous made her hold her spellbook a little too tightly against her chest, which is exactly what she was doing when she crossed the root-bridge and saw that someone had gotten there before her.

The someone was a draenei, robed plainly, staff planted in the moss with the easy confidence of a person who has never once worried about looking silly. They were watching the moonwell with the patient expression of someone who had already decided the day was going to be interesting, one way or another.
"You got a note too," said the draenei, without turning around. It wasn't really a question.
"I did," said Nova. "I don't suppose you know what it's about."

"Not the faintest idea." A pause, and then, over one shoulder: "I'm Aala. I was told to bring my staff, so either we're being tested, or somebody very important probably misplaced something very small."

Nova laughed without giving it the first thought, which she found almost as surprising as the joke itself. "Nova," she named herself, and didn't get the chance to say much else, because that was precisely the moment Conservator Ilthalaine arrived, moss-robed, staff in hand, moving like someone who had already had a very long morning, and that was the way of things and so it was just fine with her.

Now, a word about Ilthalaine. She was the sort of elder who had clearly seen every kind of trouble a forest could produce, filed it neatly away, and was fully prepared to see it all again. She did not waste words. She did not waste time. And when she pointed her staff out past the water, both apprentices understood, instantly, that whatever was wrong was wrong in a big way, and so it was to be their job to fix.

"The spring rains were generous this year," Ilthalaine said. "Too generous." Beyond the moonwell, the ferns were doing something ferns were not supposed to do, trembling with far too much traffic. A trio of thistle boars shouldered past each other like impatient customers at a very small bakery. Somewhere in the shadows, a nightsaber slid past and vanished, the way nightsabers do, as if the forest had simply blinked.
The problem was though, trembling leads to trampling and the plants of the glen were stressed. This is precisely the kind thing that gets the attention of Conservators.

"Boar and nightsaber alike have multiplied beyond what the glen can feed," Ilthalaine went on. "If they are not encouraged gently outward, they will starve, or turn on one another for what little is left."
Nova's mind, which liked things sorted into tidy piles, sorted this immediately. "So we're not hunting them. We're moving them along."

"Just so. Thin the crowded clusters. Send them to further out. Just enough of them to restore the balance." Ilthalaine looked at her, really looked, the way conservators do when they want you to remember something. "No more."
Aala's grip on their staff tightened, just slightly. "And if someone decides that enough is not enough?" they asked. "If someone decides restraint is inconvenient?"
"Then I am trusting you," said Ilthalaine, "to be the one who remembers it isn't."

That seemed to settle something in Aala, though not entirely, because Aala turned to Nova next, studying her the way you might study a stranger you've just been handed a rope and told to trust with your life. Then, apparently satisfied, Aala grinned.
"So. Do we restore balance," they said gravely. "...Or convert excess boar to bacon sandwiches?"
Nova blinked. "I'm sorry, what?"

"Nothing. Just checking you were listening." And there it was, Nova's first real look at the fact that she had just been paired, for reasons unknown, with someone who used jokes the way other people used shields.

They set off together down the root-lined path, wisps drifting between the roots like lazy lanterns, and Nova spent several strides deciding what on earth to say to a person she had known for less time than it takes to boil an egg.
"Bacon sandwiches," she said eventually, mostly to herself.
Aala laughed, a proper, delighted laugh. "Hee hee hee. Got you."
It is, I should tell you, a very unusual way to begin a friendship. But then, the best ones often begin that way.

The path soon dipped through fern beds gone ragged at the edges, not the gentle raggedness of wind and weather, but the sorry, flattened raggedness of far too many hooves. Nova crouched to look. "It's not just a few animals," she said. "There's so many squished together that they are even tramping their food."
Aala's humor dropped away like a cloak shrugged off. "Then we'll be quick," they said, "and gentle where we can."

Deeper into the woods, things only got worse. Webwood silk hung where silk had no business hanging. Boar-scars tore up the soft earth. Saplings stood stripped and bent, like they'd been leaned on by something enormous, something thoroughly unbothered about the damage it was doing. Nova and Aala slowed at the edge of a grove gone thick with all this trouble, after a moment of saying nothing at all, the pushed forward.

The clearing beyond held the worst of it, four or five thistle boars packed into a space built for one, jostling like too many people trying to use the same doorway at once, with more shapes shifting in the brush beyond.
Aala's steadiness wavered, just for a heartbeat. "So many," they murmured. "They can't help the damage they are causing."
"No," Nova agreed. "But we can. Let's get this done."

She lifted her staff. She had practiced this spell a hundred times in empty rooms, on nothing more dangerous than dust motes, and never once on anything that could run away, or worse towards her with viscious tusks. A pale glow gathered at the staff's tip.
"A gentle push is all it should take," she said. "Watch."

And she let it go, not a blow, not a blast, nothing you'd write a song about, just a slow, curling pressure that eased around the boars like a polite but very firm usher clearing a theatre. The boars startled, shuffled, and peeled away toward the wider thickets, entirely unharmed and entirely unimpressed, which is really the best outcome you can hope for from a thistle boar.
Aala let out a long breath, shoulders loosening. "With that pack moved on," they said, watching the last one vanish, "hopefully the rest will find new homes too."

For a moment, the clearing was simply quiet, and quiet, as any storyteller will tell you, is when the important things tend to happen. Aala rested a hand near Nova's shoulder careful, testing, the way you'd offer a hand to someone you weren't yet sure would take it.
"You did amazingly, Nova, just the perfect amount of surprise to see them off."

Nova felt her face go warm. "I'm so glad we didn't hurt them," she admitted, more honestly than the moment probably called for. But Aala only nodded, as though that one small admission had told them something worth knowing.
They might have lingered there longer, if Aala hadn't crouched, a breath later, beside a moss-covered root and gone very still. Four deep gouges, freshly clawed into the wood.
"Take care," Nova said, all her ease folding back into alertness. "These are nightsaber hunting grounds. They can appear out of"
She never finished the sentence, because the shadows above them chose that exact moment to move.

"EEEEEEP, it's above us!" Aala's staff came up faster than thought, and a shimmering shielding ward flared into being overhead, just as a nightsaber's leap came down toward them, all claws and shadow and considerably more angry weight than either of them wanted to think about.

Nova didn't have time to be frightened. She only had time to cast a curling ribbon of pale light spooling out from her staff, bending gently around Aala's ward, catching the nightsaber's leap and steering it sideways, as harmlessly as a kitten bumping off your leg.
"Be gone," she said, and she said it kindly, if firmly, which is a very Nova sort of thing to do even to a beast trying to eat her.

The nightsaber twisted mid-air, landed hard but whole, shook itself off with the deeply offended air of a cat that has just missed a jump on purpose, and slunk away into the trees without so much as a backward glance.
For a moment, neither of them moved. Then Aala let their breath out in one long, shaky, delighted laugh, and lowered the ward.
"I think, that's the glen cleared." they said. "GG."

Now, Nova had no idea what those two letters meant. But she understood the feeling behind them perfectly well, that giddy, wobbly-kneed relief of having done something difficult and come out the other side of it whole, standing next to someone she had met only that morning and somehow already trusted with her life. She decided she didn't need to know what it meant. She suspected she'd be hearing it again.

They walked back to the moonwell slower than they'd left it, unhurried, the whole glen settling into a calm that hadn't been there before. Ilthalaine was waiting, and turned to greet them with the look of someone who already knew, somehow, exactly how the morning had gone, as if it was already determined before they had even woken up this morning.
"You've kept the balance," she said, drawing two folded cloaks from beneath her arm, moss-and-leaf toned, plain, and entirely new. "Wear these with pride."

Nova took hers with a quiet, surprised sort of pride she hadn't expected to feel over a piece of cloth. Aala accepted theirs with a grin, shrugging off the travel cloak they'd arrived in that morning as though it belonged to someone they'd already outgrown.
"Matching cloaks," Nova said, settling hers into place, fighting a smile of her own. "Try not to make it weird."
"No promises," said Aala.

And so they stood there together at the water's edge a little longer than strictly necessary, two strangers who had walked into Shadowglen's ferns that morning, and walked out of them as something else entirely. Not quite friends yet. But you could see the shape of it forming already, plain as two matching cloaks in the moonlight.

paragraphs: Every apprentice will tell you, if you catch them off duty, away from mentors and letters home, that no spell in any spellbook is half so tiring as all of the walking. Nova had learned to freeze a puddle solid at ten paces and to coax a spark from cold flint without singeing her eyebrows more than twice, but nothing in her small wooden staff had prepared her for the particular ache of the last mile before supper.
"Tell me again," she said, "why we didn't just teleport."
"Because," said Aala, not breaking stride, "neither of us knows how, and also because you'd probably teleport us into a tree."
"That was one time."
"It was a very grumpy squirrel hiding in that tree though."

They had been Conservator Ilthalaine's errand-runners for the better part of a fortnight, carrying letters, chasing lost livestock, standing very still while older Sentinels decided whether they were trustworthy enough to be handed anything sharper than a broom. Their reward for it, besides aching feet, hung new and unfamiliar across both their shoulders: matching cloaks of deep forest green, still creased along the fold lines from wherever cloaks are kept before they're given to people who've earned them. Nova kept catching hers on branches. Aala kept catching theirs on Nova.

Ahead of them, the land dropped toward a cluster of curved timber roofs tucked into the tree line, lantern-glow just beginning to bud in a window or two. Beyond it all, and beyond everything, really, rose the vast purple hush of Teldrassil's canopy and the roots of the great tree itself, thick as castle walls, disappearing up into a sky just starting to consider becoming night. A few wisps drifted lazily along the tree line, in no particular hurry, the way wisps generally aren't.
"Hollowroot Waypost," Aala announced, in the tone of someone introducing royalty. "Home of the world's most interesting and boisterous stew and, exactly one room short of what we need."
"Comforting."
"I do try."

The stable came first: a lean-to of curved wood and leaf-worked joinery, open on one side to the evening air, holding a handful of tired mounts who'd clearly had a longer day than either of them. Aala went to one without being asked, resting a palm against its nose the way they did with anything that looked worn out, which, this week, was most things.
"There," Aala murmured. "You're not the only one who's had a long walk."
Nova watched them do it and said nothing, filing the gesture away the way she filed away most things worth remembering.

The well came next, tucked between two buildings with roofs like folded leaves. Nova set her staff against the stone rim and began hauling up water while Aala waited, arms crossed, wearing the particular look of someone about to say something they'd clearly been saving.
"Smells like stew night," Aala said. "Brace yourself, apprentice."
"I've survived worse," Nova said, hauling up the bucket. A pause. "…I think?"
"That's the spirit. Low expectations. Very wise."

Their quarters, when they found them, turned out to be less a room than a shed that had been argued into cooperating: supply crates stacked along one wall, coils of rope hanging like sleeping snakes, one lantern doing its honest best to light the whole space and mostly failing. Nova set her satchel and spellbook down atop a crate with the air of someone claiming territory.
"At least the crates make excellent shelving," she said.

Aala, unrolling a bedroll into the one clear patch of floor, didn't even look up. "Could be worse. My bunk on the ship that fled our dying home world had less legroom than this. Crate palace is a real upgrade."

It came out light, a throw away line, almost a joke, the way Aala tossed out most things that weighed more than they let on, and it landed exactly as intended, which is to say it didn't land at all. Nova laughed, because that's what you do with a joke, and neither of them said anything more about dying worlds, not yet, because the stew was calling and the stew, as established, was argumentative and boisterous.

The dining hall hit them like a wave. Long tables crammed with off-duty guards, road-worn caravan hands, and a cluster of Sentinel trainees comparing bruises; a great pot of something being ladled out at speed; carved moon-and-leaf beams overhead doing their best to look dignified above all the noise. Nova and Aala paused just inside the door the way you do before jumping into cold water.
"Here we go," Aala said, and went first.
Every bench was full in the particular way benches get full when nobody wants to be the one who scoots. Nova wedged herself into a gap with the solemnity of a diplomat opening negotiations.
"Excuse me," she said, nudging an elbow firmly aside. "Just relocating your elbow."
"Huh?" Aala jolted half an inch, genuinely startled, then grinned. "I thought you loved my elbows in your personal space."
"I tolerate them. There's a difference."
"Same thing, smaller word."
Supper arrived in a bowl that steamed with what Nova privately suspected was ambition rather than actual nutrition. She peered into it with the exact scrutiny she gave unfamiliar runes.
"Sample logged," she announced, to no one in particular, staff resting across her knees. "Broth. Root vegetable. Something structurally similar to meat."
Beside her, Aala took a spoonful, chewed, considered, and delivered their verdict with the flat calm of a Sentinel reporting a scouting patrol.
"Definitely a step up from rations on a dying world," they said. "Though don't tell Cook I said the bar was low."

It was the second time that evening the words had slipped out disguised as a joke, and the second time Nova let it pass without comment, though she noticed. Nova noticed most things. She simply hadn't yet decided what to do with this one.

Across the hall, chaos erupted in miniature: two trainees had discovered, apparently at the same instant, the same single loaf of bread (a dark, defiant, catastrophically over-toasted thing that looked as though it had survived at least one kitchen fire and held a grudge about it) and were now engaged in a tug-of-war conducted with the seriousness of a border dispute.
"Nuuuu," Nova said, mournfully. "Not the loaf again."
"Every chow time is loaf time!" Aala said, delighted, twisting around to watch. "Like clockwork. I've started taking bets on how burnt it'll be."
"You've started taking bets on bread."
"I contain multitudes."

The loaf survived, more or less, and the hall settled back into its usual roar. And it was somewhere in the lull after second helpings (the specific, companionable quiet that only happens between people who've stopped needing to fill every silence) that the noise of the room seemed to Nova to fall away, just for a moment, just around their end of the table.

"My people fled a dying world," Aala said, quietly, hands still around their bowl, "generations before I was born. When your everything is crammed into one starship, you learn to tend what's still standing." A pause, longer than their usual pauses. Then, softer, almost to themself: "Also, you learn to season stew properly. Priorities."

They said it lightly. They always said it lightly. But Nova set her spellbook aside, actually aside, actually paying attention, the small unconscious tell she had whenever something mattered, and simply listened, all the way through, joke and all, letting both halves of it sit exactly where Aala had put them.
Nobody made a speech about it. Nobody needed to.

"Mine's less noble," Nova said eventually, because it seemed only fair, and because two-handed honesty is easier than one-handed honesty. "I wasn't fleeing anything. I 'borrowed' a spellbook I wasn't supposed to read, and my mentor caught me elbow-deep in forbidden theory. Next minute, I found myself here."
Aala's grin came back full force, chin propped on one hand. "Nova and forbidden theory. That's very on-brand."
"It is not my brand."
"It is entirely your brand. It's practically your family crest."

And that was that: not a grand confession, not a solemn oath of friendship, just two apprentices trading the shapes of where they'd come from across a table that smelled like ambitious soup, and somehow trusting each other a little more for it than they had an hour before.
The loaf, meanwhile, had made a full recovery and reappeared at their own table, set down between them by whichever unlucky server had drawn the short straw.
"This," Nova said, eyeing it with deep suspicion, "is yesterday's loaf. I'd bet my staff on it."
"Don't," said Aala, already laughing. "You'll need the staff more than the bet, but props to the loaf, persistent little thing."

They laughed together, properly laughed, shoulders bumping, satchel and staff forgotten against the bench, the whole crowded hall blurring warm and amber around the one small, well-earned point of quiet between them.
"GG," Aala said at last, wiping their eyes, "to the loaf. Never change."

And somewhere above them, the carved moon-and-leaf beams held their usual dignified silence, entirely unbothered by the bread-based diplomacy unfolding underneath them, while outside, Teldrassil's ancient roots kept their equally ancient watch: patient, unimpressed, and, if you asked Nova, faintly amused.

paragraphs: Stories beneath very large trees have a habit of beginning quietly. This is because very large trees know they can afford to wait.

Aldrassil had waited through more dawns than Nova could imagine. Its colossal roots rose from Shadowglen like the backs of sleeping dragons, supporting curved wooden platforms, mossy bridges, and entire gardens that would have been forests anywhere else. Beneath its purple canopy, two moonwell pools shone through the ferns. Their silver water was so calm that the drifting wisps could admire their reflections without a single ripple spoiling the view.

Nova and Aala approached between the pools, following a path that curled around one of Aldrassil’s roots. Nova carried her simple wooden staff in one hand and kept the other near the small spellbook at her belt. She stood a little straighter than necessary, as she often did when she wished to look prepared.

Aala walked half a pace ahead. Their healing staff touched the moss with soft, regular taps, while their field satchel rested against one hip. They were watching the clearing rather than the path, which was why they noticed the figure lying on a bed of ferns before Nova did.

Dentaria Silverglade knelt beside him. The Priestess of the Moon wore flowing robes patterned with leaves and pale silver, but there was nothing ceremonial in the way she worked. One hand hovered above the injured Night Elf’s arm, holding a steady gleam of moonlit magic over his skin.
The other hand gripped her staff.
That was the first sign that something was badly wrong. Dentaria Silverglade did not seem like someone who gripped anything unless it needed gripping.
She looked up as Nova and Aala entered the clearing. Relief softened her face.
“Nova, Aala. I hear your training is going well. I am so glad you have come to help.”
Aala was already moving toward the fern bed.
“I see someone is hurt. How can we help?”

The injured Night Elf’s name was Iverron. His woodland clothes were damp with sweat, and an unhealthy grey pallor had crept across his face. His breathing came in shallow pulls, as though each breath had to be persuaded to enter and then reminded how to leave.

Dentaria drew back the edge of his sleeve. Two tiny punctures marked his forearm. They were not dramatic wounds. They hardly looked worthy of the trouble they had caused, which is often the way with venom, bad promises, and stones inside shoes.
“The webwood spiders have gone mad,” Dentaria said. “They are usually so timid, but today one bit Iverron.”
Nova crouched on the opposite side of the fern bed. Her fingers tightened around her staff as she studied the mark, the grey skin surrounding it, and the faint tremor in Dentaria’s glowing hand.
“You are keeping the venom from spreading,” she said.
“For now.”

Dentaria’s answer was calm, but the light around her fingers flickered. Nova understood what the priestess had not said. Holding the venom still was costing her strength, and strength was not an endless thing, even for a Priestess of the Moon.
Aala lowered their voice.
“What do you need?”
Dentaria reached toward a small ingredient bowl beside the ferns. Inside lay crushed leaves, clear water, and the torn remains of a luminous white flower.
“What I need are more lilies. You can find them around the edges of the ponds.”
She lifted the last whole petal between two fingers. It gave off a pearly glow, as though it had swallowed a piece of the moon and was keeping it for later.
“Moonpetal Lilies,” Nova said.
“The same. They grow north of these pools, close to the water. Bring me as many as you can carry. Quickly.”
Nova stood at once and pointed her staff toward the gleam of water between the trees.
“By the ponds, near the water. We’ll be quick.”
Aala rested one hand on their healing satchel.
“You can count on us. Back in a flash.”
This was an excellent thing to say when leaving on an urgent errand. It sounded confident, efficient, and pleasantly swift.
The forest, however, had not been asked for its opinion.

The path north wound through ferns tall enough to brush Nova’s elbows. Wisps drifted between the trunks, making small pools of light beneath the canopy. The moonwell remained visible behind them for a time, first as two silver circles and then as a broken shimmer between the roots.
Nova kept her eyes on the ground. She looked for damp soil, flattened reeds, and the faint glow of Moonpetal Lilies.
Aala watched the trees.
“Stay away from the branches,” they said. “They are covered in spiders.”
Nova glanced upward.

Webwood silk hung between the low boughs in long pale ropes. Some strands were thin enough to tremble in the air. Others had been layered until they resembled gauze curtains, wrapping entire clusters of leaves in a ghostly sheen.
“I see the webs,” Nova whispered.
“I was hoping you would also see the spiders.”

At first Nova did not. Webwood spiders could remain very still when they wished, and they usually wished to remain still whenever anything larger than themselves wandered nearby. Then one shape unfolded from the bark. Another shifted beneath a leaf. A third descended on a thread as slowly and solemnly as a very small, very hairy noble arriving at court.
More shapes stirred behind it.
Aala stopped so suddenly that Nova nearly walked into them. They extended one arm across her path and planted their staff beside the ferns.
“Go quietly, Nova. We don’t want to upset them.”
“I am being quiet.”
“You are whispering with your entire posture.”
Nova straightened, realised this proved Aala’s point, and lowered her shoulders.
The first spider crept across a strand of silk. Then another came down beside it. Their legs moved in quick, uncertain patterns, and the cluster above began to sway.
These were not the timid creatures Dentaria had described. They were restless. Agitated. Something had roused them beyond simple hunger or fear.
Nova could feel the answer prickling at the edge of her curiosity.
Unfortunately, the spiders were also prickling closer.
Aala shifted in front of her. One hand moved toward their prayer cloth, ready to raise a ward.
“We can back away,” they murmured.
Behind them, Iverron lay beneath Dentaria’s failing light. Ahead, beyond the webbed trees, the pond glimmered through the reeds.
Nova tightened her grip on her staff.
“We do not have time to take the long path.”
The nearest spider raised its forelegs.
Aala gave her a very particular look. It was the look of someone who already knew what Nova was about to do, did not approve, and was preparing to help anyway.
“Nova.”
“Okay, okay,” Nova said. “I’ll ask them politely to leave.”
She raised her staff.

The spell began as a pale blue spark. Nova guided it along the wood, gathered it above her hands, and released it in a broad curling sweep. The arcane wave passed around the spiders rather than striking them, stirring silk, leaves, and fern fronds into a sudden silver-blue gust.
The spiders scattered.

Some fled up the branches. Others dropped into the ferns and vanished beneath the broad leaves. A few swung wildly on threads before scrambling away with whatever dignity a dangling spider could collect under the circumstances.
Nova allowed herself one breath of triumph.
Then something landed on the back of her hand.
There was a quick pinch.
“Ow!”
Nova shook her wrist. A lone spider tumbled into the ferns and vanished after the others. Two small red marks remained on her skin.
“One of them bit me,” she said, staring at the punctures. “I suppose my manners weren’t so great.”
“Nova!”
Aala caught her wrist before she could hide the hand behind her back.
“It is barely anything,” Nova said.
“Let me see it.”
“I can still move my fingers.”
“That is not the comforting argument you think it is.”

The last spiders disappeared into the webbed shadows. Aala paid them no attention. They guided Nova down onto a patch of moss, set her staff aside, and opened the field satchel with the speed of long practice.
Nova’s hand had already begun to ache. The pain was not severe, but it was spreading toward her wrist in a thin, cold line. She watched Aala unfold their prayer cloth and lay it beneath her hand.
“Hold still,” Aala said. “This won’t take long.”

They cupped Nova’s fingers between their own. A gentle radiance gathered around their hands, warmer in colour than Dentaria’s moonlight but strangely cool against Nova’s skin. The chill sank through the bite, drawing the sting out with it.
Nova tried not to twitch.
Then the magic brushed the centre of her palm.
A laugh escaped her.
Aala looked up sharply. “Does it hurt?”
“No. Thank you. It is cold and it sort of tickles.”
“Terrible news. You may survive.”
The light brightened. The two punctures faded, and the grey tinge beginning around them withdrew until Nova’s skin was clear again.
Aala continued holding her hand for another moment, checking her fingers and wrist. Only when they were satisfied did they release it.
Nova turned her hand beneath the filtered forest light. No mark remained.
She could have said that the bite had been small. She could have said she had known Aala would heal it. She could have said several things designed to make the mistake sound less like a mistake.
Instead, she picked up her staff.
“Thank you,” she said quietly. “Next time I will go slowly.”
Aala raised one eyebrow.
Nova sighed. “More slowly.”
“An ambitious beginning.”
They continued toward the pond.
This time Nova watched the branches as well as the path.

The trees thinned ahead, opening around a shallow stretch of silver water. Reeds crowded its edges, their narrow leaves whispering whenever a wisp passed through them. The moonwell pools could still be seen through the roots behind them, but only just. Dentaria and Iverron were hidden by distance and ferns.
At first Nova saw nothing among the reeds.
Then a petal opened.

It was white at the centre and almost transparent at its edges. Light travelled through it in a slow pulse. Another flower glimmered beside it, then another, until the pond edge seemed scattered with fallen stars.
“Moonpetal Lilies,” Nova breathed. “She was not exaggerating. They almost glow.”
“Almost?”
Nova crouched beside the nearest flower. “I am maintaining scholarly caution.”
“Of course.”

They worked quickly but carefully. Nova loosened each stem from the wet soil without crushing the petals. Aala gathered the lilies into their open satchel, laying them across the prayer cloth so they would not bruise against the buckles.
A webwood spider watched them from a distant branch.
Nova noticed it. Her hand tightened on her staff, then relaxed.
She did not cast.
The spider remained where it was, no longer advancing, while Nova returned to the lilies.
They gathered every blossom they could reach without trampling the reeds. Soon Aala’s satchel shone through its seams, and Nova carried a final armful against her apprentice robe.
“Enough?” Aala asked.
Nova looked at the flowers, then toward the silver pools.
“It has to be.”

The return journey felt twice as long, as urgent journeys often do when someone is waiting at the other end. Nova and Aala hurried beneath the webbed branches, but Nova no longer rushed blindly. At each curtain of silk, she paused long enough for Aala to find the clearest route.
No spiders followed them.
They emerged between the moonwell pools to find Dentaria still kneeling beside Iverron. Her shoulders had begun to shake with the effort of holding the venom at bay.
Nova crossed the final stretch at a run.
“Here are all the lilies we could carry,” she said. “I hope it is enough.”
Dentaria released a breath that sounded as though she had been holding it since morning.
“These will do perfectly.”

Aala knelt and opened the satchel. Dentaria took the lilies in both hands, crushed their glowing petals into her ingredient bowl, and worked them through the prepared leaves and moonwell water. Pale light rose from the mixture in curling threads.

Nova watched every motion. She noticed how Dentaria pressed rather than tore, how she turned the bowl three times, and how the Moonpetal light changed from white to soft green when the remedy was ready.
Aala watched Iverron.
Dentaria lifted his head and touched the antidote to his lips. At first, nothing happened.
The moonwell waters remained still. The wisps drifted. Somewhere above, a wooden platform creaked beneath the immense patience of Aldrassil.
Then Iverron swallowed.
The grey pallor loosened around his mouth. Colour moved slowly across his face, faint at first, then warm and living. His breathing deepened. His fingers curled against the fern bed.
Aala leaned forward.
Nova forgot to breathe.
Iverron’s eyes opened.
Dentaria smiled, and the tiredness in her face could no longer hide the relief beneath it. Iverron looked up at her, confused but awake, and managed to close his hand around hers.
The Moonpetal light faded from the empty bowl.
“These will do perfectly,” Dentaria said again, looking toward Nova and Aala. “Thank you. Your swiftness is appreciated.”
Nova flexed her healed hand behind her staff. Aala noticed, because Aala noticed such things, but said nothing. Their small sideways smile was quite enough.

For several quiet minutes, the clearing belonged entirely to relief. Dentaria helped Iverron sit against the ferns. Aala offered him water. Nova gathered the scattered bowls and placed them within Dentaria’s reach, taking special care not to knock over anything important and therefore proving that lessons can occasionally survive longer than a few minutes.
Above them, Aldrassil’s purple leaves stirred.
The wisps changed direction.
One by one, they drifted away from the pools and moved toward the northern path.
Dentaria watched them go. The warmth left her expression, not because Iverron’s recovery mattered less, but because the forest had remembered another trouble.
She rose and turned toward the distant roots. Between them, far along the shadowed path, the mouth of a cave waited like a dark knot in the wood.
“The spirits whisper of more to be done,” Dentaria said. “Tarindrella has returned in the north. Go now to find her.”
Nova followed the wisps with her gaze.

Aala closed their satchel and stood beside her. Neither of them knew why the dryad had returned after so long, or what had driven the webwood spiders from timidity into madness. The forest had given them one answer and, as forests often do, hidden three more beneath it.
They stepped onto the northern path together.
At the first strand of webwood silk, Nova stopped.
She looked at the branch. She looked at Aala. Then she carefully walked around it.
Aala’s smile appeared at the corner of their mouth.
Nova pretended not to notice, which was difficult, because this time she was paying attention.

paragraphs: Trouble came to Shadowglen dressed in moonlight.

This was one of trouble’s less considerate habits. It never arrived wearing a sign that said TROUBLE, or rattling a bucket, or shouting from the treetops. Instead, it shimmered across silver water, drifted among the glowing wisps and waited beside the moonwell until someone sensible noticed that the forest had become much too quiet.
Dentaria Silverglade had noticed.

The Priestess of the Moon stood beneath the immense roots of Aldrassil with one hand wrapped around her moonlit staff. In the other, she held a small glass vial stopped with a wooden cork. The liquid inside was pale and clear, almost ordinary, though things carried by worried priestesses are rarely ordinary for long.

Nova and Aala stood before her in their matching forest-green cloaks. Nova held her wooden staff a little straighter than necessary. Aala had one hand near their field healing satchel, ready for Dentaria to tell them where the next injury was hiding.
“The spirits whisper of more trouble in the north,” Dentaria said. “Tarindrella has returned.”
Nova’s ears lifted.
“A dryad?” she asked. “There has not been one in Shadowglen since before the blessing of Teldrassil.”
Her eyes brightened for half a heartbeat. Then her brow tightened.
“That is exciting,” she added carefully, “and a sign that something is very wrong.”

“Both may be true,” Dentaria said. “Tarindrella waits within the Shadowthread cave. The webwood spiders there have been touched by a corruption deeper than the poison that struck Iverron. Seek her out. Help her drive back the brood and learn what has caused this.”
At the mention of poison, Dentaria held out the vial.
“Take this antidote. You may need it.”

Aala accepted it with both hands and inspected the glass against the moonwell’s glow. Then they tucked it securely into an inner pocket of their satchel, between folded bandages and a small prayer cloth.
“A cave,” they said.
Nova glanced across at them.
“Yes.”
“I hate caves.”
“You have never mentioned that.”
“I was hoping never to require an official policy.”
Dentaria’s expression softened, although only slightly. “Travel carefully. The spiders are dangerous, but they may also be victims of whatever has changed them. Do not mistake cruelty for courage.”
Aala nodded at once.
Nova’s grip shifted on her staff. “We will find Tarindrella. We will learn what happened. And we will come back.”
There are promises made because a person knows exactly what lies ahead, and there are promises made because standing silently would be unbearable. Nova’s belonged firmly to the second sort.
Still, she meant it.

North of the moonwell, the canopy thickened and the light thinned. The roots of Teldrassil rose around the path like the walls of some vast, sleeping palace. Purple leaves crowded out the sky, ferns brushed against the travellers’ knees, and the last few wisps became small silver lanterns floating between the trees.
Aala walked half a pace ahead, their healing staff ready.
“Stay close,” they said. “If something attacks, my shield will protect us.”
“Your shield protected us last time.”
“That is why I am recommending it again.”
Nova smiled faintly. “A proven strategy.”
“Exactly. Very fashionable among people who enjoy remaining unbitten.”
The path narrowed between two roots. Nova stopped so suddenly that Aala’s cloak brushed against the back of hers.

A strand of webbing hung across the hollow ahead. It was thicker than ordinary spider silk and dark enough to swallow the glimmer from Nova’s staff. Pale green flecks moved beneath its surface, blinking like sickly stars.
Nova did not touch it.
Instead, she crouched and held her staff close enough for its modest arcane light to pass over the strand.
“This silk is darker than the webbing near the moonwell,” she said. “It has been corrupted, not merely spun.”
The strand continued into the forest, tied from root to root in a broken trail.
Nova marked the nearest trunk with a tiny arcane spark. It settled harmlessly into the bark and glowed like a blue pinprick.
“The trail keeps going north. I will mark our way back.”
Aala studied the dark passage beyond.
“I approve of this plan.”
“You sound surprised.”
“I am celebrating personal growth.”

The corrupted silk thickened as they travelled. Soon it hung in curtains between the roots, and little scraps of shed carapace lay scattered across the path. No birds called from the canopy. Even the ferns seemed to lean away.
Then the root wall opened.

The mouth of the Shadowthread cave yawned before them, draped in heavy webs. Cold air spilled from it, smelling of wet stone, old leaves and something sharp enough to make Nova’s eyes water. The corrupted thread ran straight into the darkness.
Nova and Aala stopped.
The cave waited.
Caves are excellent at waiting. They have practised for thousands of years and do not become embarrassed when nobody speaks.
Aala cleared their throat.
“After you, brave heart.”
Nova looked at them. “I thought you hated caves.”
“I do. That is why I plan to enter immediately behind the person with the glowing staff.”
“Safety first?”
“Safety first.”
Nova raised her staff and stepped across the threshold.
The cave swallowed the forest light within three paces.

Their footsteps became small, wet sounds. Webbing muffled every wall and hung from the ceiling in ropes. Nova’s arcane glow caught pale shapes moving far above them, but whenever she turned the staff upward, the shapes were gone.
Aala walked close enough that their shoulders nearly touched.
“This whole nest feels wrong,” they whispered. “Not merely dangerous. Sick.”
A gentle green light appeared ahead.
It shone through several layers of webbing, soft at first, then brighter as a tall figure moved toward them. Nova raised her staff. Aala brought their healing staff across their body.
The hanging silk parted.
Tarindrella stepped into view.

Her upper body was that of an ancient woodland guardian, slender and leaf-adorned, with an ageless face and branchlike antlers. Below the waist, she possessed the graceful body and legs of a great forest deer. Moss and small leaves clung to her flanks. Green motes drifted around her, and each hoofstep awakened a curl of new grass from the barren cave floor.
Nova forgot to lower her staff.
“A dryad,” she breathed. “A real dryad.”
Tarindrella regarded her with quiet amusement. “I had hoped to remain one.”
“My mentor will never believe this.”
“Then you must take great care to return and argue with them.”
Aala lowered their staff, though not entirely. Their gaze had moved past Tarindrella to the blackened webbing.
“Dentaria sent us,” they said. “She told us the spiders were corrupted.”

“She was wise to send you.” Tarindrella’s expression grew sorrowful. “The sickness has spread through the brood. These creatures once fled from footsteps and fed quietly beneath the roots. Now they attack anything that moves. They tear at the forest, and at one another.”
Something clicked in the darkness behind her.
Then another something answered.
Tarindrella turned toward the sound. “We must drive them from the passages and discover the source before the corruption spreads beyond this cave.”
Aala’s eyes remained fixed on the shifting webs.
“We subdue them where we can,” they said. “Whatever is hurting them, it is not their fault. They are not choosing this.”
Tarindrella studied Aala for a long moment.
“No,” she agreed. “They are not.”
A shape burst through the webbing.
The spider was larger than a nightsaber cub, with a dark carapace veined by green light. It sprang directly at Tarindrella, legs spread and fangs bared.
Nova’s staff flashed.

Her arcane bolt passed beside the spider rather than through it, bursting against the cave wall in a crack of blue light. The blast turned the creature in midair. Aala’s translucent ward flared beneath it, guiding its fall away from the group, while vines erupted from the stone and wound around its legs before it could spring again.
The spider struck the ground in a tangled heap, furious but unharmed.
More eyes opened in the dark.
Three spiders rushed from the left. Two dropped from the ceiling. A smaller one skittered behind Nova and found itself staring into an arcane circle that had appeared beneath its feet.
Nova tightened both hands around her staff.
“Back,” she commanded.
The circle pulsed. The spider slid across the stone as neatly as a bowl pushed along a table, coming to rest inside a curtain of sticky webbing.
Aala’s ward spread over Nova just as another creature struck from above. Its claws scraped against the golden surface without reaching her.
“Remember,” Aala called, bracing their staff, “they are frightened and sick!”
“I remember!”
“Just checking!”
Tarindrella swept one arm upward. Roots cracked through the cave floor and curled around the attacking spiders, lifting them away from the trio and binding them gently but firmly against the walls.
Nova spotted a gap between Aala’s ward and the roots. Another spider was gathering itself to leap.
She drew a breath.
The spell in her staff shook once. Fear climbed from her hands into her shoulders, whispering that the cave was too dark, the spider too fast and she was still only a beginner playing at bravery.
Then she noticed the spider’s weight shift onto its hind legs.
She saw the angle of the jump.
Nova turned her staff by the width of two fingers and released the spell.
The arcane pulse struck the ground just in front of the creature. Stone dust leapt upward. The spider recoiled into Tarindrella’s waiting vines and was bound beside the others.
Nova stared at it.
Her spell had gone exactly where she intended.
“Me and this staff,” she said, with considerably more confidence than she had possessed three seconds earlier, “we can handle anything.”
Aala gave her a sidelong look from behind the ward.
“Sure,” they said. “Of course you can.”
Tarindrella’s vines tightened as the captured spiders struggled. The dryad moved among them, touching neither fang nor carapace. She knelt beside the first creature and held one hand above it.
Green light passed from her palm into the spider.
The creature shuddered. Beneath its shell, thin veins of corruption answered with a poisonous glow.
Tarindrella’s face became very still.
“This taint was not caught from the webbing,” she said. “It lies too deeply within them.”
Nova crouched nearby, watching the light travel through the spider’s body. “How deeply?”
“These spiders were born carrying it.”
Aala’s expression changed from concern to anger, though theirs was a quiet anger, the kind that shuts doors carefully because it is saving its strength for something more important.
“The eggs,” they said. “The broodmother passed the corruption to them.”
Tarindrella rose. Behind her, a passage sloped deeper into the cave.
“Githyiss the Vile nests at the far northern end. If the corruption is bred through the brood, then we will find its beginning with her.”
Nova looked along the passage. The webbing there was so thick that it seemed less like silk and more like the pale skin of some enormous buried thing.
“We came to find the source,” she said.
Aala adjusted their satchel. The antidote vial gave a tiny glass clink within it.
“And apparently to improve my relationship with caves.”
“Is it improving?”
“No.”
They followed Tarindrella north.

The passage narrowed until Tarindrella had to fold her antlers through curtains of silk. Egg sacs hung from the ceiling, each one trembling faintly. The stone beneath their feet grew colder, and the corrupted green glow became bright enough that Nova no longer needed her staff for light.
That did not make the place more welcoming.
It merely allowed them to see exactly how unwelcoming it was.
At the edge of a vast chamber, Tarindrella stopped.
Aala touched Nova’s arm.
“Breathe,” they said softly. “Together, we can do this.”
Nova realised she had been holding her breath and let it out.
Then they entered the lair.
Githyiss the Vile rose from the far wall.

She was enormous. Her abdomen was swollen beneath plates of sickly carapace, and her legs unfolded one after another until she towered above the chamber floor. Corrupted webbing streamed from her body and stretched into every tunnel. Hundreds of smaller spiders clung to the walls around her, packed so closely that the stone itself seemed to ripple.
When Githyiss struck the ground with one foreleg, dust fell from the ceiling and every egg sac began to sway.
If she had sneezed, she might have rearranged the cave.
Tarindrella planted her hooves.
“I will hold Githyiss,” she said. “You must keep her offspring away from me.”
Aala looked from the broodmother to the army covering the walls.
“I dislike plans that begin with ‘I will hold the enormous spider.’”
“Then it is fortunate,” Tarindrella replied, “that it is my plan.”
Githyiss lunged.

Tarindrella swept both arms forward. Roots tore through the chamber floor and wrapped around the broodmother’s foremost legs. Githyiss ripped one free, but three more vines took its place. Green light blazed across the cave as dryad and spider strained against one another.
The offspring poured down the walls.
Aala struck the base of their staff against the stone. A broad ward sprang up around them and Nova, glowing warm gold against the sickly darkness.
The first wave struck the barrier.
Nova raised her staff.
“You shield,” she called. “I’ll attack!”
“Way ahead of you,” Aala answered. “They’re all yours.”

Nova did not need to ask where Aala would move. She felt the ward shift before each opening appeared. One moment it curved left, turning aside a cluster of claws. The next it narrowed at the front, giving Nova a clear path for her magic.
She sent controlled pulses into the stone and webbing around the spiders. Each blast drove them sideways, backwards or up into Tarindrella’s smaller vines. None struck flesh. None needed to.
A spider dropped behind Aala.
Nova turned.
Aala ducked before she called a warning.
Nova’s spell passed over their horns and severed the web strand above the creature. A heavy curtain of silk fell across it, wrapping it from legs to fangs.
Aala looked back.
Nova raised one eyebrow.
“Of course you did,” Aala said.
The broodmother wrenched another leg free. Tarindrella staggered, one hoof scraping across the stone. Githyiss reared over her, fangs dripping venom.
Aala expanded the ward.

The golden barrier caught Githyiss’s descending legs and held them just long enough for Tarindrella to recover. Roots burst upward in a great twisting cage, binding the broodmother’s body without piercing her shell.
“Be still, poor thing,” Tarindrella said through clenched teeth. “Your suffering ends here.”
Githyiss shrieked.
The sound rushed through the chamber, and every smaller spider froze.
In the sudden stillness, Nova saw a light that did not belong.
It pulsed beneath a mound of webbing behind Githyiss. The colour was wrong even for corruption, thicker and yellower, shining in hard, regular beats.
“There,” Nova said. “Under the webbing. That glow is not coming from the cave.”
Tarindrella glanced toward it, but Githyiss strained against her bonds. “I cannot release her.”
“You do not need to,” Aala said.
Their ward bent into a narrow shield before Nova.
Nova understood immediately.

Aala advanced, carrying the shield with them. Nova stayed close behind. Spiders crowded in from both sides, only to be diverted by the moving wall of light or swept into coils of loose silk by Nova’s carefully placed spells.
They reached the mound.

Nova slid the end of her staff beneath the outer layers of webbing. She sent a thin arcane shimmer along the wood, loosening the sticky strands without setting them alight. Aala held the ward steady as claws scraped across its surface.
“Almost,” Nova said.
“I would enjoy ‘now’ more than ‘almost.’”
Nova twisted her staff.
The webbing tore open.
A crude wooden face stared back at them.

The carving had a broad snout, small round ears and heavy brows, closer to the head of a bear than to any elf or draenei. Twisted cords and teeth hung around its neck. Sickly light seeped through cracks in the wood and crawled into the surrounding silk.
Tarindrella saw it from across the chamber.
“Gnarlpine,” she said.
The word carried more weight than a shout.
Nova looked at the network of glowing webbing. Every strand led back to the totem.
“It has been feeding the corruption into the nest.”
“And through Githyiss into her eggs,” Aala said.
The broodmother thrashed again. Her movement pulled the webbing tight around the totem, and the carved face flared brighter.
Nova placed both hands on her staff.
“I can free it, but I need the ward closer.”
“You have it.”
Aala stepped beside her. The barrier folded around them like a shell.

Nova gathered her magic into one fine, steady line. It would have been easier to release a great blast. Great blasts are popular with inexperienced mages because they make a tremendous noise and give everyone the impression that something decisive has happened.
Nova had begun to understand that precision was often braver.
Her spell moved through the webbing strand by strand, severing each connection without touching the creatures trapped nearby. The totem’s light flickered.
Tarindrella drove her hands downward.
A root erupted beneath the carving and curled around it. Wood groaned against living wood. The totem tore free of the cave floor.
The sickly light went out.
Not dimmed. Not hidden.
Out.

Githyiss sagged into the cage of roots. Across the chamber, the smaller spiders stopped clawing at Aala’s ward. Some folded their legs beneath themselves. Others retreated into the shadows, bewildered and trembling.
The egg sacs ceased to glow.
For several breaths, nobody moved.
Then Aala slowly lowered their staff.
Nova’s spell faded from hers.
Tarindrella kept the totem sealed inside a knot of roots. Without its light, it looked small and ugly, the sort of thing that might have been kicked aside on an ordinary forest path.
That was another of trouble’s habits. Once uncovered, it was often much smaller than the fear it had grown around itself.
Tarindrella approached Githyiss. The broodmother remained bound, but her frantic movements had stopped. Her many eyes followed the dryad with dull exhaustion instead of fury.
“The corruption has loosened its hold,” Tarindrella said. “It has not undone all the harm, but the brood is no longer being driven by it.”
Aala moved among the bound spiders, checking each one from a careful distance.
“They will live?”
“Most will. They will wake frightened, hungry and exceptionally bad-tempered.”
“That sounds healthier.”
Nova looked back at the root-wrapped totem. “Why would the Gnarlpine place it here?”
“To poison the brood,” Tarindrella said. “Or to poison the forest through them. I cannot yet say.”
Beyond the lair, a darker passage continued north.
Tarindrella turned toward it.
“I will follow their trail. When you return to Dentaria, tell her what we found. Then seek Athridas Bearmantle in Dolanaar. He knows the griefs of this forest and may know what the Gnarlpine intend.”
“You are going alone?” Nova asked.
“I travel more swiftly through root and branch than either of you.”
Aala folded their arms. “That was not the question.”
Tarindrella’s solemn expression warmed. “I will travel carefully.”
Nova suspected this was what experienced guardians said when they had no intention of being sensibly supervised.

Tarindrella extended one hand. Nova placed hers against it, and Aala added theirs above Nova’s. Dryad, Night Elf and Draenei stood together in the dim chamber while the quieted brood shifted around them.
“You fought with mercy when fear offered easier choices,” Tarindrella said. “Shadowglen will remember that.”
Aala released her hand first and checked their satchel. The antidote vial was still secure, never opened and never needed.
Nova noticed.
“Does carrying the antidote all the way through a spider cave count as using it responsibly?”
“It counts as not being poisoned,” Aala said. “I strongly recommend the experience.”
Tarindrella stepped into the northern passage. Green motes followed her between the roots until the darkness swallowed them one by one.
Nova and Aala turned south.

Behind them, Githyiss rested within Tarindrella’s living cage. The sickly light had vanished from the egg sacs, and the webbing no longer twitched as though the cave itself were angry. Ahead, far beyond the tunnels, the moonwell waited beneath Aldrassil.
They had entered the Shadowthread cave as two beginners following a trail.
They left it knowing where the other would stand when darkness came rushing at them.
The forest had answered one question and grown three more in its place, which is how forests ensure that adventurers never become too comfortable.
Aala adjusted their satchel. The unused vial chimed softly inside.
Nova lifted her staff.
Together, they followed the blue marks home.

paragraphs: The cave did not so much release them as reluctantly stop holding on.

Nova stepped through the mouth of Shadowthread first, blinking as ordinary afternoon light poured across her face. Behind her, the cave sank into a cold tangle of stone and webbing, its corrupted brood at last fallen silent. Ahead waited the familiar ferns and colossal roots of Shadowglen, all glowing beneath Teldrassil’s purple canopy as though enormous spiders had never existed and the forest had spent the day doing nothing more alarming than growing moss.

Aala emerged next, one hand on their healing staff and the other hovering near the field satchel at their side. They took a careful breath, listened for pursuing legs, and then let their shoulders loosen.
Tarindrella came last.

The dryad crossed from darkness into sunlight with the quiet grace of a deer stepping through water. Leaves and trailing vines stirred in her hair. The bark-toned skin of her arms was scratched with cave dust, but she carried herself as straight and watchful as any ancient tree.
For a little while, none of them spoke.

After the broodmother’s cavern, the sounds outside seemed almost impossibly small. A wisp hummed between the roots. Somewhere overhead, a bird argued with another bird about a matter of tremendous importance known only to birds. Wind moved through the canopy in one long, leafy sigh.
Nova looked back at the cave.
“The totem is still in there,” she said.
“So is the broodmother,” Aala replied.
Nova turned away at once. “An excellent reason not to go back for it.”
Tarindrella studied the forest to the north. The warmth that had entered her expression upon reaching daylight faded, and her long ears tilted towards something Nova and Aala could not hear.
“The Gnarlpine will have left other traces,” she said. “I am going north to find their stronghold and learn how far this corruption has spread.”

Nova tightened her hand around her wooden staff. Part of her wanted to offer to go too. It was the same part that considered every closed door an invitation and every ancient warning an unfinished research note.
Tarindrella looked at her before she could speak.

“Your path lies elsewhere for now,” the dryad said. “If you need me, seek Athridas Bearmantle in Dolanaar. He knows the paths beyond Shadowglen, and he listens more carefully than most people with Bearmantle in their name.”
Aala raised an eyebrow. “Try not to vanish into the woods forever this time.”
A smile flickered across Tarindrella’s face.
Nova stood a little straighter. “We will see you again, Tarindrella. I am sure of it.”
The dryad inclined her head, accepting the certainty as though it were a promise worth keeping. Then she turned north.
The forest gathered her in.

First the ferns hid her hooves. Then the dappled shadows crossed her flanks, breaking her outline into patches of bark and leaf. One moment Tarindrella was there, slender and unmistakable beneath the roots. The next there was only undergrowth swaying where she had passed.
Aala peered after her.
“She really does enjoy an exit.”
Nova adjusted the strap of her satchel. “Perhaps dryads practise them.”
“That would explain a great deal.”

They set off for Dentaria Silverglade’s training glade, following the gentler trail south. Their forest-green cloaks were dusty, their steps were slower than they had been that morning, and Nova discovered that every dangling vine looked exactly like a spider leg when glimpsed from the corner of her eye. This was inconvenient because Shadowglen contained approximately nine million dangling vines, and the forest had made no effort whatsoever to label the harmless ones.
By the time silver moonwell light appeared between the trees, Nova had stopped flinching at seven of them.

Dentaria stood beside the water in her flowing robes, sorting dried herbs into small bundles. The Priestess of the Moon looked up as Nova and Aala entered the clearing. Her weathered composure broke into open relief.
“You have returned,” she said, hurrying towards them. “It is good to see you both safe.”

Aala accepted Dentaria’s inspection with the patience of someone who knew that healers considered the word safe a theory requiring extensive testing. Dentaria checked their hands, searched their face for hidden pain, and glanced towards the satchel where the small unused antidote vial still rested among bandages and prayer cloth.
Nova received the same treatment next.
“We are unhurt,” she said.
Dentaria gave her a look suggesting that apprentices had made similar claims shortly before collapsing throughout recorded history.
“Mostly unhurt,” Nova amended.
Dentaria’s gaze softened. “You have dealt with the source of much of what plagued this part of the forest. Shadowglen owes you both more than you know.”
“Just a few spiders,” Aala said. “Barely broke a sweat.”
Nova stared at them.
“A few spiders? One was bigger than a mammoth!”
“An unusually leggy mammoth.”
“It had fangs.”
“Some mammoths may have private lives we know nothing about.”
Dentaria covered a smile with one hand, though not very successfully. For a moment, the danger of the cave seemed to loosen its grip on all three of them.
Then the priestess looked towards the moonwell.
“You have done well,” she said, “but before you leave Shadowglen, one rite of training remains.”
Nova’s expression sharpened at once.

Dentaria took a small glass phial from the folds of her robe. It was plain and narrow, sealed by a fitted stopper. No runes decorated it. No jewels caught the light. It looked rather ordinary for something being presented with such ceremony, which meant it was almost certainly not ordinary at all.
She placed it in Nova’s palm.
“Northeast of this glade lies an older moonwell,” Dentaria continued. “Its shrine is secluded beneath the roots. Go there respectfully, draw a phial of its water, and return it to me intact.”
Nova turned the empty vessel between her fingers. “Is the water dangerous?”
“No.”
“Unstable?”
“Not in the way you mean.”
“Guarded by anything enormous?”
Dentaria glanced at Aala.
“I believe you have encountered enough enormous things for one day.”
Aala nodded solemnly. “A wise policy.”

Dentaria folded Nova’s fingers around the phial. “The moonwell may offer you a glimpse of our history and our magic. Do not try to command what it shows. A memory is not a spell to be forced into shape.”
Nova’s serious expression brightened despite all her efforts to contain it.
“History, dryads, magic,” she said. “Can this day get any better?”
“Possibly,” Aala replied. “If it had started at a beach with a nice cold...”
“The path is northeast,” Dentaria said, though her eyes were smiling.
Aala sighed. “The forest conspires against refreshments.”
They departed before the afternoon could grow old enough to become evening.

The path northeast began broadly, winding between the familiar fern beds and curved wooden platforms of the training grounds. Soon it narrowed beneath roots that had risen from the earth in great twisting walls. Moss softened the stones. The canopy thickened overhead, turning the daylight darker and more golden.
Nova carried the phial inside her satchel, wrapped in a clean cloth and positioned where her spellbook could not crush it. She checked this arrangement three times in the first ten minutes.

“I wonder what kind of magic Dentaria meant,” she said. “Old wards, perhaps. Or an enchantment preserved in the water. It might respond to the glass, or to whoever collects it, or to a particular phase of the moon.”
“Or it may be simpler,” Aala said.
Nova looked across at them. “Simpler than a moonwell containing centuries of magical history?”
“A place worth remembering can have magic of its own.”
“That is not a measurable category of magic.”
“Not everything needs to fit in your spellbook.”
“My spellbook has several blank pages.”
Aala’s sideways smile appeared. “Of course it does.”

The deeper they travelled, the less the forest seemed interested in helping them hurry. Roots crossed the trail at inconvenient heights. Ferns leaned over the path as if attempting to hear their conversation. Once, Nova paused beside a stone marked with faint curling patterns, only for Aala to point out that the marks had been made by a snail with a surprisingly ambitious sense of direction.
At last the path curved beneath a vast arch of living wood.
Beyond it rested the older moonwell.

It was nothing like Dentaria’s open training glade. Moss-covered stones formed a low, sunken circle beneath the roots. Silver water filled the basin almost to its rim, perfectly still except where pale wisps drifted above it. No platforms overlooked the shrine. No voices carried from nearby paths. The place seemed to have been sitting alone for centuries, patiently waiting for visitors who understood that silence was not an empty thing.
Nova stopped beneath the arch.
Even Aala had no joke ready.

The silver light caught the edges of their forest-green cloaks and turned them pale. Great roots enclosed the shrine without smothering it, creating walls, pillars and a roof that no carpenter could have planned. The air smelled of wet stone and leaves after rain.
Nova removed the wrapped phial.
Aala looked from her to the moonwell, then took one respectful step back.
“You go on,” they said. “This belongs to your people. I will keep watch.”

Nova had expected Aala to come to the water with her. They had entered caves together, faced corrupted beasts together and stood beneath the broodmother’s shadow without needing to discuss which of them would shield and which would strike. Yet somehow Aala understood that sharing every danger did not mean claiming every moment.
“Thank you,” Nova said.
Aala rested both hands upon their staff. “I will be right here.”
Nova approached the moonwell alone.

She knelt on the mossy stone and set her wooden staff beside her. For a moment she simply watched her reflection. The young Night Elf in the water looked more tired than she had expected, her reward cloak rumpled and her eyes too bright with questions.
Dentaria had told her not to command the memory.

Nova knew many ways to command magic. She could give a spell a shape, a direction and, on particularly successful occasions, a destination that was not her own sleeve. Waiting without reaching for control was considerably more difficult.
She breathed in.
Then she lowered the phial.
The moonwell stirred before the glass touched it.

A ring of light spread across the surface. It passed beneath Nova’s reflection, erasing the tired apprentice and replacing her with silver brightness. The wisps rose together. Water curled around the phial without spilling, filling it in one smooth shining thread.
Nova froze.
The light climbed her hand.
It flowed over the stone rim, through the moss and up the surrounding roots. The shrine did not disappear, but another place unfolded within it, delicate as an image held beneath clear water.
Ancient Kaldorei figures stood beneath a much younger sky.

They wore ceremonial robes and carried silver lamps, shallow bowls and staffs adorned with living leaves. At their centre grew a young World Tree, not yet colossal, not yet broad enough to hold villages among its branches. It was a sapling by the measure of such trees, slender and luminous, its leaves trembling in moonlight.
The priestesses did not raise their arms in triumph. They did not call down storms or blaze with terrible power. They kept watch.

One tended a lamp whose flame had grown low. Another carried water to the roots. Some stood silently with their hands folded. Others looked tired, yet remained. Their patience filled the vision more completely than any spell.
Seasons passed in a breath.

Moonlight became rain. Rain became sunlight. New leaves unfolded. The watchers changed, but the watching did not. Each figure seemed small beneath the growing tree, almost impossibly small, yet every cup of water, every guarded night and every quiet act of care became part of something larger than any one of them could have seen.
Nova forgot the phial in her hand.
For one heartbeat, the grove remembered everything it had ever been.

She felt the age of the roots around her. She felt the distance between her own brief life and the long memory of her people. Yet she also felt the weight of the little glass vessel she had been trusted to carry, and understood that history was not made only by heroes whose names survived in songs.
Sometimes it was made by whoever stayed awake to tend the lamp.

Behind her, Aala shifted their stance as the silver light rose, but they did not rush forward. One hand moved towards the healing satchel. Their gaze stayed fixed on Nova, ready to act if wonder turned to danger, yet trusting her to remain within the moment.
The vision faded gently.
The ancient priestesses became columns of moonlight. The young tree dissolved into the reflection of roots overhead. The last silver leaves scattered across the water and vanished without a sound.
Nova remained kneeling.
The filled phial shone in her hand.
Aala waited until Nova stood and replaced the stopper. Only then did they come closer.
“I saw them,” Nova said. Her voice sounded too small for the shrine, but the roots listened anyway. “The first priestesses. They were keeping watch before any of us were born.”
Aala studied her face rather than the glowing water.
“What did it feel like?”
Nova looked back at the moonwell. It had settled once more, quiet and unreadable.
“Like being small,” she said slowly. “But also important at the same time.”
Aala nodded as if this answer made perfect sense.
Nova wrapped the phial carefully, tucked it into her arcane satchel and tested the fastening twice. Then, after considering the age and dignity of the shrine, she tested it once more.
“Come on,” Aala said. “Let us get that water to Dentaria before it gets ideas of its own.”
Nova glanced at the satchel.
“Do you think it might?”
“No, but you looked as though you were preparing to begin a twelve-part investigation.”
“It would have been eight parts at most.”
“That is why we are leaving now.”

The path back seemed shorter, as return journeys often do when no enormous spiders are involved. Evening had begun to soften the forest. Gold light slipped between the roots, and the purple canopy deepened overhead.
Nova spoke little. She did not need to. The memory travelled with her, steadier than the water in its padded cloth.
Dentaria was waiting beside her moonwell when they entered the training glade.
Nova crossed to her and removed the phial with both hands. Its silver contents caught the first hint of evening and held it.
“Here,” Nova said. “Thank you for showing me that. Everything I saw, I will remember.”
Dentaria accepted the phial, but her attention remained on Nova.
“Then you have already learned the lesson.”
Aala joined them at the water’s edge. “Does completing the lesson involve sitting down?”
“It may,” Dentaria said.
“Excellent. I am beginning to understand Night Elf traditions.”
Nova watched Dentaria place the phial within a carved wooden holder beside the moonwell. The vessel had returned intact, exactly as she had promised. The task was finished.
Yet something within her had not ended with it.
Dentaria looked beyond the glade. Through a break in the roots, the vast trunk of Aldrassil rose into the evening, its spiral path climbing towards the heights.
“One task remains before you leave Shadowglen for the wilds beyond,” she said.
Nova and Aala followed her gaze.

The day had already contained a corrupted cave, a dryad’s farewell, a mammoth-sized spider, an ancient shrine and a memory older than any of them. By sensible standards, this should have been enough adventure for several days and possibly a small festival.
Nova’s fingers tightened around her staff.
Beside her, Aala gave a long, theatrical sigh, then smiled.
Together they looked towards Aldrassil.
The moonwell water was no longer Nova’s to carry.
The memory was.
