paragraphs: Every great tree has at least one path that goes on longer than good manners should permit.
Aldrassil had several.

The longest was a broad wooden ramp that curled around the colossal trunk in an ever-rising spiral. Its railings had been coaxed from living branches, its boards fitted between roots as thick as houses, and its upper turns vanished among leaves that seemed to have misplaced the sky.
Nova and Aala had been climbing it for some time.
“How many times have we gone around the tree?” Aala asked.
“Seven,” said Nova.
“You counted?”
“I began counting after the third.”
“Of course you did.”
Nova adjusted the strap of her arcane satchel. The small glass phial inside it gave the faintest tap against her spellbook, and her hand immediately pressed against the flap to steady it.
Aala noticed. Aala noticed most things, particularly things Nova hoped nobody had noticed.
“It is still there,” they said.
“I know.”
“And still sealed.”
“I also know that.”
“And yet you have checked it twelve times.”
“Thirteen.”

The phial had begun its journey at an ancient moonwell, where Nova had lowered it into water bright with memories older than Shadowglen. She had seen the first Kaldorei priestesses tending their lamps beneath a young World Tree, each of them patient, watchful and small beneath the spreading branches.
Dentaria Silverglade had listened to Nova’s account without interrupting. Then she had placed the filled phial back into Nova’s hands.
The blessing was not meant to remain with her, Dentaria had explained. It had to be carried onward to Tenaron Stormgrip at Aldrassil’s summit.
That was how blessings often behaved. They arrived looking like gifts, stayed just long enough to become responsibilities, and then demanded to be taken up an enormous tree.

The ramp curved again. Shadowglen lay far below them now, softened by distance into silver ponds, fern beds and purple-black canopy. The paths Nova and Aala had travelled during their training looked impossibly small from above. Somewhere among those leaves was Dentaria’s moonwell. Somewhere beyond it lay the Shadowthread cave, quiet for the moment but not yet cleansed of every secret.
Nova paused beside the railing.
Aala stopped with her.
“It does feel strange,” Nova admitted.
“The height?”
“The leaving.”
They looked down together. Their matching forest-green cloaks stirred in the open air, two modest scraps of colour against the tremendous bark.
Aala rested both hands across the top of their healing staff. “We have not left yet.”
“No,” said Nova, looking up at the ramp’s next turn. “Apparently the tree intends to keep us forever.”
At last, the spiral opened onto a broad summit platform.

The air changed first. Beneath the canopy, every breath had carried damp moss, bark and fern. Up here it carried clear sky. Late-afternoon sunlight spread across the platform in long golden bands, and beyond the curved railings the crown of Teldrassil rolled away in every direction.
An elderly Night Elf stood at the far edge.

Tenaron Stormgrip was tall even with age stooping his shoulders. Silver moon patterns crossed his deep-hued robes, and a moonstone pendant rested over his chest. One hand held a ceremonial branch-staff polished smooth by many years of use. The other lay lightly upon the railing as he watched the forest below.
He turned before either traveller spoke.
“Nova,” he said. “Aala. You have taken your time.”
“The ramp took most of it,” said Aala.
Tenaron’s mouth creased with quiet amusement. “It has always believed that wisdom should be uphill.”
Nova stepped forward and opened her satchel. She withdrew the phial with both hands, careful not to grip it too tightly.
“Dentaria said this was meant for you.”
Tenaron received it with the solemnity of someone accepting far more than water. Silver light shifted inside the glass, gathering around his fingers.
“This gift has a habit of finding its way to where it is needed,” he said. “I think that is why it so rarely travels alone.”
His gaze moved from Nova to Aala, and some of the formality left his face.
He raised the phial between his palms.
“Be still a moment. The old magic works slowly.”
Aala settled beside Nova. Neither spoke.

Tenaron closed his eyes. The silver embroidery on his sleeves caught the light, then seemed to return it. A faint glow formed inside the phial, no brighter than moonlight upon a shallow pool. It spread through the water in fine threads, curling and joining until the whole vessel shone.
Nova felt her breath shorten.

For one heartbeat she remembered the luminous procession at the ancient moonwell: shallow bowls carried through the grove, patient lamps, leaf-adorned staffs and the slender shape of a young World Tree reaching upward. She had felt small in that vision, but not unimportant. A single lamp was small. So was a single bowl of water. Yet the grove would have been darker without either.
Beside her, Aala stood perfectly still. Their hand had moved to the strap of their healing satchel, a familiar gesture whenever feeling threatened to become visible.
The glow faded slowly. Tenaron opened his eyes.
“Our people sometimes mistake age for wisdom,” he said. “The two are acquainted, but they are not the same thing.”
He returned his attention to Nova.
“You carry our people’s curiosity like a torch. You will do great things for the Kaldorei, and for this world.”
Nova’s fingers tightened around her wooden staff.
She had prepared herself for instructions, warnings, corrections and perhaps a small lecture concerning the proper transport of sacred liquids. She had prepared no defence at all against praise.
Tenaron turned to Aala.
“And you did not need Kaldorei blood to earn our respect. Shadowglen is safer for your kindness. We thank you.”
The summit became very quiet.
Aala looked past Tenaron toward the distant canopy. Their glowing eyes had gone suspiciously bright.
Nova searched for a response, found several inadequate ones and attempted to say all of them at once.
“I don’t know what to say. I mean, I do, obviously. Thank you. I’ll remember every word.”
Tenaron inclined his head.
Aala drew a careful breath. “Careful, Tenaron. Keep talking like that and I’ll probably cry.”
“Then I shall stop,” said Tenaron. “A flooded summit would be inconvenient.”
Aala’s crooked smile arrived at last.

Tenaron crossed to a low stone table near the centre of the platform. Upon it rested a small ceremonial vessel worked in silver leaves and crescent shapes. He removed its stopper and poured the consecrated water from Dentaria’s phial into it.
The stream seemed to hang in the air for an instant, silver and unbroken. When the last drop fell, the new vessel gave a soft musical note.
Tenaron sealed it and placed the empty phial beside his staff.
“What you began in Shadowglen does not end here,” he said. “There is much more to learn throughout Teldrassil, and beyond it in Darnassus.”
He offered the silver vessel to Nova.
“Corithras Moonrage awaits at Dolanaar’s moonwell. This carries what you brought me, now prepared for him.”
Nova accepted it and inspected the stopper.
Once.
Then twice.
Aala raised an eyebrow.
Nova placed the vessel inside her satchel, wrapping it carefully in her spare cloth and positioning her spellbook beside it as a brace.
Tenaron pointed across the canopy. Far below, a pale road wound from Aldrassil’s roots and vanished beneath the trees.
“Follow the road south. Where the cobblestones turn, go west. Dolanaar lies beyond the bend.”
His expression grew grave.
“Stay on the road. Dangerous beasts have been active in the woods of late.”
Aala nodded. “Stay on the road, beasts are cranky. Understood.”
Then they looked at Nova.
“Think you can resist collecting a rare plant specimen?”
“I do not collect every rare plant I see.”
“You stopped halfway through a cave because the moss was growing in an unusual direction.”
“It was important moss.”

Tenaron watched this exchange with the patient expression of a keeper who had seen many promising adventurers and suspected that most of them survived through a combination of courage, friendship and somebody remembering to bring bandages.
“Go carefully,” he said.
Nova and Aala bowed their farewells. Then they returned to the ramp and began the long descent.
Going down was faster, though not nearly fast enough for Aala’s liking. By the time they reached the final curve, the sunlight had lowered and the forest beneath them had deepened from green to gold.
They passed between Aldrassil’s great roots and stepped onto the open road.
Aala looked back.
The vast tree rose behind them, its platforms and railings already half-hidden among the leaves. Shadowglen lay beyond those roots, with its moonwells, familiar paths and quiet shelters.
“Feels strange, doesn’t it?” they said. “Leaving the only home we’ve had here.”
“A little,” Nova replied. “But we’re not leaving Dentaria behind. Just her moonwell.”
“That is a very Nova way to look at it.”
“Is that good?”
“I have not decided yet.”
They continued south.
Tenaron’s words travelled with them.

Words sometimes do that. The most important ones refuse to stay where they were spoken. They climb into a pocket or a satchel and follow for miles, making themselves heavier or lighter depending on how a person carries them.

Nova had first felt the old keeper’s praise settle upon her like another responsibility. Great things sounded enormous. Great things sounded as though they required ceremonial robes, flawless spells and a dramatic understanding of where to stand during thunderstorms.
But the road asked for none of those things.
It asked her to keep walking.
It asked her to notice the loose stones.
It asked her to protect a small vessel of water.
Curiosity like a torch, Tenaron had said. A torch was not the sun. It did not have to illuminate the whole world at once. It only had to show the next few steps.
Nova’s shoulders loosened.

Aala’s silence was different. They were still thinking about blood, belonging and the peculiar weight of being thanked by people whose oldest traditions had begun long before the draenei ever reached Azeroth.

They had expected to be tolerated in Shadowglen. Then they had hoped to be useful. Respect had felt like something that might come later, after years of proving themselves and making no embarrassing mistakes in sacred places.
Tenaron had spoken as if it had already happened.
Aala touched the edge of their green cloak. It was dusty, slightly frayed and unquestionably theirs.

The road narrowed as the canopy thickened overhead. Cobblestones pressed through moss and soil, pale beneath their boots. Wisps flickered between distant trunks, appearing and disappearing like stars that had wandered too close to the ground.
Nova checked her satchel.
Aala caught the movement.
“If you trip and spill it,” Nova said before they could speak, “I will hide in these woods forever.”
“You are the one carrying it.”
“I am describing the general consequences.”
“Then hand it over before your imagination materialises fantasy into reality.”
“That is not how arcane magic works.”
“You say that with remarkable confidence for someone who once borrowed a forbidden spellbook.”
Nova moved the satchel to the side farthest from Aala’s reaching hand. “You are never going to let that story rest, are you?”
“Stories need exercise.”
The road sloped gently downward. Afternoon thinned into evening, and long shadows stretched across the stones. At last the cobblestones curved west exactly as Tenaron had promised.
“There,” said Nova. “The turn.”
“Good. I was beginning to suspect we had somehow missed an entire direction.”
They had taken only a few steps beyond the bend when Aala stopped.
Their staff struck the road with a quiet knock.
Nova stopped beside them.
At the edge of the trees, a low branch had been snapped cleanly from its trunk. The leaves had not yet wilted. Above it, four deep claw marks scored the bark, each one longer than Nova’s hand.
Something heavy had disturbed the undergrowth. Ferns lay crushed beside the road, leading into the dark between the trees.
“Something big passed through here,” Nova whispered.
“And recently.”
Aala’s voice had become softer. Their stance widened, and one hand slid toward the Woven prayer cloth tucked beneath their belt.
“Be alert. Clearly Tenaron wasn’t exaggerating.”

Nova studied the marks. The cuts were fresh, but no sap moved within them. Whatever had made them had climbed or stretched high against the trunk. The crushed plants led away from the road rather than toward it.
She listened.
Leaves shifted somewhere in the distance.
A branch creaked.
Nothing emerged.
“Whatever it was, I think it’s gone,” Nova said. She took her staff in both hands but did not raise it. “I’ll keep this handy all the same.”
Aala nodded.

Neither suggested following the trail. This was worth noting, because several weeks earlier Nova would almost certainly have used the words brief investigation, which are the traditional opening words of many avoidable disasters.
They remained on the cobblestones.

For a while, the forest seemed to move beside them. Shadows kept pace between the trees. Small sounds became large ones: the scratch of bark, the tumble of a pebble, the sudden wingbeat of a bird hidden high overhead.
Nova kept her magic close and controlled. Aala watched the darker side of the road, ready to place themselves between danger and their companion.
The sounds gradually fell behind.
The path widened.
A lantern appeared between the trees ahead.
Aala lowered their staff. “GG, forest. You had us worried for a minute there.”
Nova stared at them. “Did you just congratulate the forest for not eating us?”
“Good sportsmanship matters.”
“To the forest?”
“It did its best.”
Another lantern appeared, then another. The trees opened, revealing curved wooden roofs gathered around a pool of silver light.

Dolanaar was smaller than Shadowglen. Its paths were shorter, its trees stood farther apart and its buildings nestled close together as though sharing the evening’s warmth. Modest market stalls lined the main road. A pair of hitching posts stood beside a hall with leaf-shaped windows, and villagers carried baskets or shuttered their shops beneath the deepening dusk.
At the village centre shone a moonwell.
It was smaller than the pools beneath Aldrassil, but its light was just as bright. Silver radiance rested upon the nearby buildings and turned every drifting leaf into a pale little boat.
“We made it,” Aala said.
Nova touched the satchel. The vessel remained secure.
“We made it with all the water.”
“An achievement historians will struggle to describe adequately.”
They approached the moonwell.

An elderly Night Elf stood at its edge, dressed in pale robes woven with silver accents. He had the calm bearing of someone who understood that water, people and ancient magic all revealed more when they were not hurried.
He turned as Nova and Aala came near. His gaze moved from their green cloaks to their road-dusted boots, then settled upon Nova’s satchel.
“Sent by Tenaron, were you?” he asked.
Nova brought out the silver-worked vessel and held it toward him.
“We carried this from Aldrassil. The water came from an older moonwell in Shadowglen.”
The keeper accepted it. Silver light moved across the vessel’s leafwork, and his expression warmed.
“I am Corithras Moonrage,” he said. “We have much to talk about.”
He stepped aside and gestured toward the glowing pool.
“But first, come. There is a lesson in this moonwell for you both.”
Nova and Aala exchanged a glance.
They were tired. Their feet ached, their cloaks carried half the road’s dust, and somewhere behind them a large beast was probably sharpening its claws upon another perfectly innocent tree.
Still, they stepped forward.
The vessel rested safely in Corithras’s hands. The road had delivered them where they were needed, just as the old blessing had delivered itself through theirs.

In the moonwell’s silver surface stood the reflections of two beginner adventurers: a Night Elf mage whose curiosity no longer felt like something she needed to apologise for, and a Draenei priest beginning to believe that belonging might be earned through kindness rather than blood.
Behind them lay Shadowglen.
Ahead waited Dolanaar, Corithras’s lesson and every road that might follow.
For the moment, that was more than enough.

paragraphs: Dusk had settled over Dolanaar by the time Corithras Moonrage led Nova and Aala to the moonwell.

It was the sort of dusk Teldrassil did particularly well. The sky between the colossal branches had faded to violet, the lamps beneath the curved roofs were waking one by one, and the first stars looked down through the leaves as though they had heard something interesting was about to happen.

Nova’s forest-green cloak was dusty from the road. Her plain apprentice robe had collected at least three leaves, one burr, and a twig that had somehow lodged itself beneath her travel belt without permission. She carried her simple wooden staff in one hand and kept the other near the small spellbook at her side.

Aala walked beside her in their matching cloak and novice priest’s robe, their healing staff grounded with each quiet step. Their field satchel rested against one hip. They looked tired, but Aala had a particular way of being tired that still suggested they could bandage someone, calm an argument, and make a pointed observation about both before sitting down.
Corithras stopped at the water’s edge.

The elderly Night Elf keeper wore pale robes woven through with silver. Moonwell light caught in those threads and made them gleam like frost upon spider silk. His expression was calm and knowing, which was a useful expression for a moonwell keeper and an extremely irritating one for anyone hoping to guess what he was about to say.
Nova glanced into the water. It was brighter than the evening sky and perfectly still.
“You promised us a lesson,” she said.
“So I did.”
“About the moonwell?”
“Among other things.”
Aala looked sideways at Nova. “You asked one question and received an answer containing three more.”
“I noticed.”
“I knew you would.”
Corithras’s smile deepened. He gestured to the pale stones beside the pool.
“Kneel here,” he said, “and let the water show you what it remembers.”

Nova’s fingers tightened around her staff. She had knelt beside another ancient moonwell beneath Aldrassil and seen the first priestesses watching over a young World Tree. She still carried that memory like a silver seed somewhere behind her ribs. It had made her feel small and important at the same time, a combination she had not yet found a sensible name for.
This moonwell felt different.
The water was not waiting quietly. It was listening.
Aala noticed the change in her posture. They always did.
“Do you want me beside you?” they asked.
Nova considered the question. This was a Kaldorei rite, but Corithras had invited them both. Aala had travelled the whole road to Dolanaar, faced the same dangers, and carried the same dust.
“Yes,” Nova said. “Please.”

They knelt together at the edge, companions rather than reflections of one another. Nova rested her staff across her knees. Aala placed their healing staff within easy reach and settled one hand over the small prayer cloth tucked into their belt.
Corithras remained standing behind them.
For several breaths, nothing happened.
Then a ripple crossed the water.

It began at the centre of the pool, though nothing had touched it. A second ripple followed, and then a third. The circles widened until silver light slipped over the rim and painted Nova’s hands, Aala’s horns, and the old keeper’s robes.
Something moved beneath the surface.
Nova leaned closer.
The water rose.

It did not splash or spill. It lifted in long ribbons, winding together into the shape of a robed figure. The figure’s face was ancient and serene. Its body remained translucent, silver-blue light forming ceremonial robes while faint starlight shone through its chest and out again.
The Shade of the Kaldorei opened its eyes.
Nova forgot to breathe.
Aala remembered for both of them.
“In,” they murmured. “Then out.”
Nova obeyed.
The Shade smiled as though it had watched nervous apprentices forget basic functions for thousands of years and had never once grown tired of it.
The village faded.

The buildings, lamps, bridges, and evening trees dissolved into silver mist. Even Corithras disappeared from view. Nova still felt the stone beneath her knees and Aala’s steady presence beside her, but the world around them had become an older place.
An empty ceremonial dais stood beneath tall boughs.

Its carved stones were beautiful, but the beauty had gone cold. No leader stood upon them. Kaldorei elders gathered below, their faces turned towards the vacant place as if absence itself might speak.
The Shade’s voice moved through the vision like wind through distant leaves.
“When Malfurion Stormrage was lost to our people, our immortality was lost with him. The druids who remained were scattered, leaderless, and desperate for a path forward.”

Nova stared at the empty dais. She had read histories in which great names marched neatly from one event to the next, every decision polished smooth by time. This was not neat. The elders shifted uneasily. Some argued. Some bowed their heads. Some simply watched the place where certainty ought to have been.
The vision changed.
The grove gave way to a windswept coastal bluff. Darkshore’s sea stretched beyond the cliffs, grey and restless beneath a low sky. Ancient standing stones rose among wind-bent grasses.
A robed Archdruid stood with his back to Nova and Aala. He raised an antlered staff before a semicircle of druids.
“Fandral Staghelm gathered those who remained,” said the Shade. “He carried his hope to the Circle of Ancients and asked them to believe that what had been lost might yet be remade.”

The gathered druids did not all look convinced. Hope, Nova discovered, was not always bright. Sometimes it stood in bad weather with mud around its boots and demanded that frightened people make a decision.
“Did they trust him?” Nova asked.
The Shade turned its luminous face towards her.
“Enough to try.”
The bluff shifted around them. The druids now stood in a circle around a single seed resting upon an ancient stone.
It was smaller than Nova expected.

Most objects that changed the world ought, by common sense, to be enormous. They ought to arrive with banners, trumpets, and at least one person announcing them in a voice trained specifically for announcements.
This seed would have fitted in Nova’s palm.
Light pulsed inside it.

The druids raised their hands. Roots of green-gold magic spread across the stone and down into the earth. Wind rushed inland from the sea, carrying salt, rain, and the deep groan of something waking far below.
Nova felt the sound through her knees.
Beside her, Aala lowered one hand to the ground. Their expression had become intent and solemn. They could feel it too.
The seed split.
A pale shoot burst from its shell.

It climbed towards the sky, slender for only the briefest instant. Then it thickened. Roots plunged into the cliffs. Branches unfolded with the roar of sails opening in a storm. Leaves streamed into being by the thousand, then the million, their light spreading over the coast.
The druids became tiny figures at the base of the growing trunk.
The young World Tree rose beyond them.

Up it went, past the standing stones, past the cliffs, past the clouds. Its roots gripped the earth while its boughs claimed the heavens. Valleys formed between them. Moonlit groves opened across the vastness of its crown. Rivers found new paths through soil that had not existed moments before.
Teldrassil was born before Nova’s eyes.
Not as a monument carefully built stone by stone, but as a living answer hurled against sorrow.

The light became so bright that Nova lifted an arm across her face. Her reward cloak snapped behind her in a wind that belonged to the vision. Aala remained beside her, one hand braced upon the ground and the other holding their prayer cloth against their chest.
The Shade stood within the radiance.
“From root to bough, Teldrassil rose,” it said. “Born of grief and defiance both.”
The words settled into Nova more deeply than any date or name.
Grief and defiance both.
She understood defiance. Defiance acted. It gathered druids, planted seeds, raised trees, and told the future it would not be allowed to arrive unchallenged.
Grief was harder. Grief did not solve anything. It remained when all the clever work was finished.
The vision moved forward.

The blinding radiance softened into twilight. Teldrassil stood whole and immense, its crown spreading beneath the stars. Villages rested among its branches. Lanterns shone along winding roads. Moonwells gleamed in hidden groves.
It looked triumphant.
Then one silver leaf loosened from a branch.
The leaf drifted down before them. Its edges had curled. Its pale surface had begun to wilt.
Aala watched it fall.
Nova felt the answer before the Shade spoke it.
“Yet even here,” the spirit said, “our immortal lives were not restored.”
The leaf landed upon the water that had appeared beneath their knees.
No matter how vast the tree became, the loss remained inside its story.
The Shade approached them across the moonwell’s surface. Each step sent faint constellations trembling through the water.
Nova looked up. “Then Teldrassil failed?”
The spirit regarded her without anger.
“No.”
“But it did not restore what they intended.”
“No.”
Nova frowned. The two answers sat awkwardly together, refusing to arrange themselves into a tidy conclusion.
Aala’s voice was quiet. “Something can save people without giving them everything they hoped for.”
The Shade turned towards them. Its ancient expression softened.
“It falls to hearts like yours now,” it said, “to find the way we could not.”

Nova felt her posture straighten. Tenaron Stormgrip’s words returned to her from the summit of Aldrassil. He had said she would do great things for the Kaldorei and for the world. She had managed to receive that prediction with only a modest amount of flustered staring.
This felt heavier.
“We are beginners,” she said.
Aala glanced at her. “A stirring declaration of confidence.”
“It is a relevant fact.”
“It can be both.”
The Shade’s smile held no mockery.
“All who begin are beginners.”
Nova suspected this was the kind of sentence ancient spirits kept ready for occasions when young people attempted to escape destiny by pointing out their lack of experience.
The spirit closed its eyes.
Its luminous form began to loosen into threads of light. Robes became ripples. Hands became falling sparks. The last thing to fade was its peaceful face.
The water took it back into memory.
Dolanaar returned all at once.

Evening lamps glowed beneath the curved roofs. Leaves drifted through the village. Somewhere beyond the moonwell, a trader was closing a wooden shutter with more banging than the shutter could reasonably deserve.
Nova remained kneeling.
Aala sat back upon their heels. Their hand rested near Nova’s shoulder, not touching, simply present.
Corithras stood behind them exactly where he had been, although Nova had the uncomfortable feeling that much more than a few moments had passed.
The moonwell became still.
Nova looked down at her own reflection. It was the same face she had brought to the water, but it did not feel arranged in quite the same way.
Corithras waited.

Moonwell keepers, Nova was learning, were very good at waiting. It was likely part of their training. Perhaps there was an examination in which candidates had to stand beside a pool for seven hours while an apprentice tried to find the correct question.
At last Nova said, “Did the Shade mean that we should restore the Kaldorei’s immortality?”
“Perhaps,” said Corithras.
“Or that we should continue searching?”
“Perhaps.”
“Or that every generation must find its own answer to what was lost?”
Corithras’s smile returned. “Perhaps you should eat before attempting the remaining possibilities.”
Aala rose and offered Nova a hand.
“He is wise,” they said.
“He has avoided all my questions.”
“He has redirected them towards dinner. That is a recognised form of wisdom.”

Dolanaar offered them a small guest room in a curved timber hall near the moonwell. It had two simple cots, a washbasin, pegs for their cloaks, and a table that leaned slightly towards the door as though hoping to escape.

Their evening meal was vegetable stew, dark bread, soft cheese, and sliced moonberries. The stew steamed between them. For a time, neither spoke. They were too hungry, too tired, and too full of thoughts, which is a crowded condition even before someone adds soup.
Nova ate half her bread before opening her spellbook.
Aala looked at it.
Nova paused. “I am only making a note.”
“You said that the last time you made six pages of notes.”
“They were concise pages.”
“One of them had a diagram.”
“The diagram prevented a seventh page.”
Aala dipped their bread into the stew. “Then civilisation owes it a debt.”
Nova smiled despite herself. She turned to a clean page but did not yet touch quill to paper.

“Immortality,” she said. “Gone. An entire people rewriting their history around losing it. The political consequences alone must have been enormous. The changes to druidic leadership, cultural memory, succession, magical research. I could study it for a lifetime.”
Aala watched her across the table.
Their expression was gentle, but there was a small crease between their brows.
“Or,” they said, “you could feel sad for them for a moment before you study it.”
Nova’s quill stopped above the page.
The room seemed to become very quiet.
Her first instinct was to explain that study and sadness were not mutually exclusive. She had several excellent arguments ready. They formed an orderly queue behind her teeth.
Then she remembered the empty dais.

She remembered the druids standing in the rain because someone had offered them a hope too desperate to ignore. She remembered the tiny seed and the immense tree. Most of all, she remembered the single wilting leaf falling through everything they had built.
Nova set the quill down.
“Right,” she said. “Sorry.”
Aala did not tell her she had nothing to apologise for. They did not rescue her from the discomfort.
Nova sat with it.
“It really is sad, isn’t it?”
“Yes.”
“They made something extraordinary.”
“They did.”
“And it still could not give them back what they had lost.”
“No.”
Nova looked towards the window. Beyond the glass, the moonwell shone between the dark village buildings.
Aala’s fingers tightened slightly around their bowl.
“My people know a little about losing what we cannot get back,” they said.
Nova turned towards them.
Aala did not often speak of their people’s exile. When they did, the words came carefully, as though carried in a vessel that had already cracked once and could not be dropped again.
Nova closed the spellbook.

She did not ask for names, dates, routes, or causes. Those questions could wait. Instead she listened while Aala spoke of departure without a promised return, of places remembered more clearly than they could ever be reached, and of communities learning to carry home within one another when the ground beneath home was gone.
They did not speak for long.
They did not need to.

When the bowls were empty, Nova washed them while Aala straightened the cots. Their cloaks hung side by side on separate pegs, still carrying the dust of the road. Nova placed her staff and spellbook beside her own bed. Aala set their healing staff and field satchel beside theirs.
The last lantern burned low.
Before lying down, Nova opened her spellbook once more. She wrote only four words.
Grief and defiance both.
Then she closed the book.
Morning found Dolanaar quiet.

Mist rested in the hollows between the roots. The moonwell had faded from brilliant silver to the pale gleam of an early sky. Villagers opened stalls, swept pathways, carried baskets, and performed all the small tasks by which a place proves it intends to continue existing.
Nova and Aala stepped from the guesthouse with their packs secured and their forest-green cloaks settled over their shoulders.
Corithras waited near the moonwell.
“Sleep well?” he asked.
“Eventually,” Nova said.

“Good. There is someone else in Dolanaar who has been waiting for news like yours. Seek out Athridas Bearmantle. He knows this forest’s troubles better than most, including, I suspect, the trouble that sent you here.”
Nova looked at Aala.
“Tarindrella mentioned that name.”
Aala adjusted their satchel. “Then let us not keep him waiting any longer than we already have.”
They started along the curved village path.
After several steps, Nova glanced back at the moonwell. Its surface was calm again. No shade rose from it. No ancient vision opened.
A single ordinary leaf drifted down and landed upon the water.
Nova felt the urge to explain what it meant.
She let herself feel it first.
Then she turned towards Aala, Athridas Bearmantle, and whatever trouble waited beneath the trees.
Together they walked into the morning.

dialogueLines.text: Or you could just feel sad for them, for a moment, before you study it.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: ... Right. Sorry. It really is sad, isn't it.

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: My people know a little about losing what we can't get back.

pages.storyFunction: Morning's direction

panels.title: Morning Comes
panels.caption: Morning found Dolanaar quiet, its moonwell pale in the early light.

dialogueLines.speaker: corithras
dialogueLines.text: Sleep well? Good. There's someone else in Dolanaar who's been waiting on news like yours. Seek out Athridas Bearmantle. He knows this forest's troubles better than most including, I suspect, the one that sent you here.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: Tarindrella did mention that name.

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: Then let's not keep him waiting any longer than we already have.

episodes.title: Nova and Aala 08 - Ashes of Starbreeze
episodes.subtitle: Shadowglen Beginnings — Book Five, Part One
episodes.sourceName: Nova and Aala/Nova and Aala 08 - Ashes of Starbreeze/Nova-and-Aala-08-Ashes-of-Starbreeze.pdf-project.json

pages.storyFunction: Briefing: the ask

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: You're doing the thing again, checking your spellbook's still there.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: It walked off once. I'm allowed to be careful.

panels.title: Athridas Arrives
panels.caption: Gaerolas Talvethren, Great Warden of Ban'ethil Barrow Den, has kept watch over its sleeping druids for as long as anyone can remember.

dialogueLines.speaker: athridas
dialogueLines.text: Good, you're both still here. Gaerolas has sent a report every day for years. Three days now, nothing.

dialogueLines.speaker: athridas
dialogueLines.text: If harm's found him, those druids may lie unguarded. Will you find him and bring back word?

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: Of course. Which way?

pages.storyFunction: Travel, steady rhythm

panels.title: The Golden Road
panels.caption: On the road east to Starbreeze Village, the last place Gaerolas was seen.

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: Wrong way, my cute little friend, there's only trouble that way!

panels.title: An Easy Stretch
panels.caption: For a while, the road felt almost easy, full of warm sunlight and good conversation...

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: You're doing the thing with your grip again.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: Gaerolas has never once missed a check-in. Three days now. It must be bad.

pages.storyFunction: Discovery payoff: the ruin

panels.title: Smoke on the Wind
panels.caption: The smell of smoke reached them before the village came into view.

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: Fan out slow. Eyes on the tree line.

panels.title: The Tree Line Breaks
panels.caption: Then the trees broke, and they saw where the smoke was coming from.

panels.title: Starbreeze in Ruin
panels.caption: Starbreeze Village. No birds. No voices. Only tracks in the mud.

pages.storyFunction: Investigation, parallel action

dialogueLines.speaker: gaerolas
dialogueLines.text: Thank the stars. I knew Athridas would send help.

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: Don't sit up. Just tell us slowly what happened.

dialogueLines.speaker: gaerolas
dialogueLines.text: The Gnarlpine did this. Their chieftain, Ursal the Mauler, had his sanity consumed by fel moss. It's driven the whole tribe mad.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: This is fel moss, and it's spreading fast and wide, it's already here in Starbreeze.

pages.storyFunction: Kinetic transition

panels.title: The Long Run Home
panels.caption: With Gaerolas stable and resting, there was no more time to lose. Athridas needed to hear this now.

pages.storyFunction: Grave report

panels.title: The Full Account
panels.caption: They told him everything. Starbreeze in ruins, Gaerolas wounded but stable, and the Gnarlpine behind it all, led by their corrupted chieftain, Ursal the Mauler.

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: Ursal's corrupted by fel moss. It's spreading through the whole tribe.

dialogueLines.speaker: athridas
dialogueLines.text: By the stars. This is quite disturbing indeed.

dialogueLines.speaker: athridas
dialogueLines.text: Rest tonight. Tomorrow I'll ask far more of you than a report.

pages.storyFunction: Ceremonial reward, closing

panels.title: The Moonwell's Blessing
panels.caption: That evening, Corithras Moonrage called them to the water's edge.

dialogueLines.speaker: corithras
dialogueLines.text: You go toward greater danger than you've yet known. Take these.

dialogueLines.speaker: corithras
dialogueLines.text: Keep this close when danger's real, Nova. It will help your spells hold steady.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: Thank you, Corithras. I won't forget it.

dialogueLines.speaker: corithras
dialogueLines.text: And for you, Aala, ring this, and your wards will rise faster and hold stronger.

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: Thank you. I'll keep us all a little safer for it.

episodes.title: Nova and Aala 09 - The Barrow Den
episodes.subtitle: Nova and Aala 09 - The Barrow Den
episodes.sourceName: Nova and Aala/Nova and Aala 09 - The Barrow Den/Nova-and-Aala-09-The-Barrow-Den.pdf-project.json

pages.storyFunction: Bridge: time passes, word arrives

panels.title: Two Days of Waiting
panels.caption: Two days passed since their warning reached Athridas. Long enough that the new gifts no longer felt so strange in hand.

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: Getting the hang of this yet?

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: Getting there.

panels.title: The Scout's Report
panels.caption: Then a Sentinel scout reached Dolanaar, breathless, with word from the west.

dialogueLines.speaker: athridas
dialogueLines.text: Then we've no more time to spare. Nova, Aala, with me.

pages.storyFunction: Briefing: the dual task

dialogueLines.speaker: athridas
dialogueLines.text: I've spent these two days consulting the ritual itself. The Barrow Den is worse than we feared. I need the Relics of Wakening from its sacred chests, but even blessed, the ritual won't take unless Ursal himself falls.

panels.title: The Relics Named
panels.caption: Four relics, four sacred chests: the Raven Claw Talisman, the Black Feather Quill, the Sapphire of Sky, and the Rune of Nesting.

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: Four chests, one furbolg-infested den. We'll manage, we always do.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: Relics and Ursal. We won't come back until both are done.

dialogueLines.speaker: athridas
dialogueLines.text: Go carefully. And go together.

pages.storyFunction: Travel, rising tension

panels.title: West Toward Ban'ethil
panels.caption: West of Dolanaar, toward Ban'ethil Barrow Den.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: Still trying to work out the kinks in this new bauble. It's working better than yesterday at least.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: More moss. The trail's thick with it, we're close.

panels.title: The Den Mouth
panels.caption: Ban'ethil Barrow Den. Once a sanctuary. Now a wound in the hillside.

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: Stay close.

pages.storyFunction: Tarindrella's reunion

panels.title: A Familiar Silhouette
panels.caption: Tarindrella, the dryad who once fought beside them against Githyiss stood waiting at the den's edge, exactly where she said she'd be.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: Tarindrella! You found the stronghold.

dialogueLines.speaker: tarindrella
dialogueLines.text: I said I would come once I found it. Ban'ethil is worse than I feared.

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: Feels like old times already. Good to have you back.

dialogueLines.speaker: tarindrella
dialogueLines.text: I could say the same. Shall we?

pages.storyFunction: Descent + combat-lite montage

panels.title: Into the Lower Den
panels.caption: The Lower Den swallowed the daylight almost at once.

dialogueLines.speaker: tarindrella
dialogueLines.text: Watch the corners. They've grown bolder since I was last here.

panels.title: Furbolg Resistance
panels.caption: Nova's frostbolt cracked past one attacker while a pulse of Aala's purifying light staggered another.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: Furbolg, incoming!

dialogueLines.speaker: tarindrella
dialogueLines.text: I'll hold the flank.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: 'Tis but a scratch.

dialogueLines.speaker: tarindrella
dialogueLines.text: That claw was corrupted. We can't just shrug it off.

panels.title: Cleared
panels.caption: The furbolg scattered, but the fight left its mark.

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: Once we've got real light and a moment's peace, I'll see to that properly.

pages.storyFunction: Relic retrieval + care beat

panels.title: The Sacred Chests
panels.caption: Four sacred chests, exactly as Athridas described, hidden deep in the Lower Den.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: One down. The Raven Claw Talisman.

panels.title: Sapphire and Rune
panels.caption: Two more chests, two more relics.

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: This is what I've been saving it for. Hold still.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: The moonpetal lily antidote, thank goodness we still have it.

dialogueLines.speaker: tarindrella
dialogueLines.text: Wait, what's this? A shaman's totem.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: Better bring it. Might matter later.

pages.storyFunction: Oben's ghost, the terrible choice

panels.title: A Ghost in the Den
panels.caption: A translucent figure drifted from the shadows, a night elf druid, both there and... not.

dialogueLines.speaker: oben
dialogueLines.text: Please don't be afraid. I need your help more than you know.

dialogueLines.speaker: oben
dialogueLines.text: That charm, was used in the shaman's ritual. I can sense it's evil.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: This is what separated you from your body?

dialogueLines.speaker: oben
dialogueLines.text: My own body walks these halls, animated and empty. To free me, you must still it, and only then use the charm upon it.

pages.storyFunction: The mercy, the release

panels.title: A Mercy, Not a Kill
panels.caption: There was no fight in it. Only a slow, deliberate act of release.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: The binding's arcane, laced through the whole body. I can see where it holds.

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: Then let it go gently.

dialogueLines.speaker: oben
dialogueLines.text: Free, at last. My thanks to you both. May we meet again, in a kinder hour.

pages.storyFunction: Deeper descent, Ursal briefing

panels.title: The Path to the Cleft
panels.caption: With the druid at peace behind them, the party proceeded into the den. The further they went, the corruption got thicker.

dialogueLines.speaker: tarindrella
dialogueLines.text: Ursal holds up in a place they call the Cleft, north from here. I've scouted the approach, he's not alone.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: This is it, then.

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: Together, like always.

pages.storyFunction: Ursal fight, building intensity

panels.title: Into the Cleft
panels.caption: The Cleft opened into a wide hollow, and there, amid broken furbolg banners, Ursal the Mauler waited.

dialogueLines.speaker: tarindrella
dialogueLines.text: Go! I'll keep the rest off you!

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: Polymorph sheep. Fingers crossed, I've only managed this twice before!

panels.title: Aala's Cry
panels.caption: A wave of dread rolled outward, and the last of the furbolg fled.

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: Begone, all of you!

panels.title: Ursal Charges
panels.caption: Ursal's charge came like an unstoppable landslide.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: There, his club's stuck and guard's down!

pages.storyFunction: The decisive blow, immediate aftermath

panels.title: The Decisive Blow
panels.caption: Frostbolt and holy fire converged, and the corruption's hold broke at last. Ursal the Mauler fell still.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: Together... now!

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: Smite!

panels.title: The Moss Recedes
panels.caption: As if a held breath finally released, the fel-moss around them began to wither and fade.

dialogueLines.speaker: tarindrella
dialogueLines.text: Is it done?

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: It wasn't easy, but it's done.

pages.storyFunction: Farewell + road coda

dialogueLines.speaker: tarindrella
dialogueLines.text: Ursal's fall doesn't end this. The corruption's root lies deeper still, I mean to find it.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: When you need us, you have but to call and we will be there. What you are doing is for the good of everyone.

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: Feels wrong, watching her go alone.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: She's not alone. She's got a whole forest listening for her.

panels.title: The Road Cleared
panels.caption: A few scattered Gnarlpine ambushers still prowled the road home. This time, they were dealt with quickly, and without a scratch. Skills were improving.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: Frost Nova, that should hold them while we slip by.

panels.title: Dolanaar in Sight
panels.caption: Dolanaar's lanterns glimmered ahead, and for a moment, the road felt almost easy again.

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: Let's see if I've gotten better at this.

dialogueLines.speaker: aala
dialogueLines.text: I have to say, it looks better than the Persistent Tavern Loaf of Longevity. How cool is that you mages can conjure food?

pages.storyFunction: Return, closing warning

dialogueLines.speaker: nova
dialogueLines.text: All four relics, Ursal released, it's done.

dialogueLines.speaker: athridas
dialogueLines.text: The Druids of the Talon may finally wake in peace. You've done what I feared impossible.

panels.title: A Deeper Warning
panels.caption: Tarindrella was already following the scent, but that road belongs to another day.

dialogueLines.speaker: athridas
dialogueLines.text: Yet Ursal was not the root of this corruption. Somewhere in this forest, the true source still festers.
